lq.q: Explain the architecture and key features of the Intel 8086 microprocessor.
answer: 1. Introduction

The Intel 8086 is a 16-bit microprocessor introduced by Intel in 1978. It marked a major advancement in microprocessor design, serving as the foundation for the x86 family of processors. It is capable of addressing 1 MB of memory and supports multiprogramming, modular design, and efficient instruction execution.
2. Architecture of 8086
The 8086 architecture is divided into two main functional units:
(A) Bus Interface Unit (BIU)
Handles all data and address transfers between the processor and memory/IO.
Functions: Instruction fetching from memory. Queuing instructions in a 6-byte instruction queue (pipelining). Segment and physical address calculation.
Instruction fetching from memory.
Queuing instructions in a 6-byte instruction queue (pipelining).
Segment and physical address calculation.
Components: Segment Registers: CS (Code), DS (Data), SS (Stack), ES (Extra). Instruction Pointer (IP): Holds the offset of the next instruction. Address Generation Circuitry.
Segment Registers: CS (Code), DS (Data), SS (Stack), ES (Extra).
Instruction Pointer (IP): Holds the offset of the next instruction.
Address Generation Circuitry.
(B) Execution Unit (EU)
Executes instructions fetched by the BIU.
Functions: Decoding instructions. Performing arithmetic and logical operations. Controlling program flow.
Decoding instructions.
Performing arithmetic and logical operations.
Controlling program flow.

Components: ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) – Performs arithmetic and logical operations. General Purpose Registers: AX, BX, CX, DX (can be divided into 8-bit halves: AH/AL, BH/BL, etc.). Pointer and Index Registers: SP, BP, SI, DI. Flags Register: Holds status flags (Zero, Carry, Sign, Parity, Auxiliary Carry, Overflow, etc.) and control flags (Direction, Interrupt Enable, Trap).
ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) – Performs arithmetic and logical operations.
General Purpose Registers: AX, BX, CX, DX (can be divided into 8-bit halves: AH/AL, BH/BL, etc.).
Pointer and Index Registers: SP, BP, SI, DI.
Flags Register: Holds status flags (Zero, Carry, Sign, Parity, Auxiliary Carry, Overflow, etc.) and control flags (Direction, Interrupt Enable, Trap).
Pipelining: While the EU executes one instruction, the BIU pre-fetches the next instruction, improving execution speed.
3. Key Features of 8086
Word Length: 16-bit processor (can process 16-bit data at a time).
Memory Addressing: 20-bit address bus → can address 1 MB of memory.
Registers: General-purpose (AX, BX, CX, DX). Segment registers (CS, DS, SS, ES). Special-purpose (IP, SP, BP, SI, DI). Flags register (status + control).
General-purpose (AX, BX, CX, DX).
Segment registers (CS, DS, SS, ES).
Special-purpose (IP, SP, BP, SI, DI).
Flags register (status + control).
Instruction Queue (Pipelining): 6-byte instruction queue enables faster execution.
Operating Modes: Minimum Mode – single processor environment. Maximum Mode – multiprocessor environment (with coprocessors like 8087).
Minimum Mode – single processor environment.
Maximum Mode – multiprocessor environment (with coprocessors like 8087).
Instruction Set: Rich set including data transfer, arithmetic, logic, control transfer, string operations, and bit manipulation.
Rich set including data transfer, arithmetic, logic, control transfer, string operations, and bit manipulation.
Clock Speed: Typically 5–10 MHz.
I/O Handling: Supports both memory-mapped and I/O-mapped devices.
Compatibility: Basis for later x86 processors, ensuring backward compatibility.
